The Future of Iran Lies Beyond the Regime
item.description:
The U.S. administration is pursuing its latest strategy: a naval blockade combined with aggressive “Outcast” sanctions, aiming to strangle the Iranian economy, force the regime to its knees, and compel it to return to negotiations on American terms.

Simultaneously, Washington is deploying additional military assets to the region. This is being framed as deterrence, but functions instead as yet another ultimatum. Any significant escalation, or even the credible threat of renewed strikes, risks triggering IRGC retaliation against critical Gulf energy infrastructure. While IRGC missile and drone inventories have been diminished, and exact IRGC munition levels remain classified, the regime likely maintains more than enough asymmetrical firepower to inflict massive damage before being neutralized.

Meanwhile, Tehran prevaricates, dodges, and plays for time. All while playing the victim, weaponizing scarcity, and brutalizing its own population. Their calculation is simple: endure enough short-term pain, while cynically passing the full brunt of it onto the Iranian people, to outlast Washington’s political tolerance.

Threats to the Strait of Hormuz and claims of control over shipping are manufactured leverage to be traded away at the right moment. They know this is opposed by virtually the entire world. By eventually “conceding” on this demand, a classic, predictable negotiating technique, they hope to secure what they truly seek: regime survival, proxy retention, and unimpeded continuation of their nuclear program.

These two paths clearly conflict with one another. Only one will prevail. But in the end, allowing an emboldened, empowered, nuclear-threshold regime to survive on their terms is utter strategic failure.

I vote for the U.S. winning. For the fall of a malignant regime that cares only about its power and wealth and holds its own people hostage.

There are no good options here. No simple fixes for where we find ourselves. Anyone with eyes can see that. So, then what?

A Radical Proposal

Forget talking to the regime. Speak to the Iranian people. Directly. Without hyperbole and with brutal candor.

Prepare them for what is coming. Not with hysterical rhetoric of annihilation, false promises of “boots on the ground,” or premature calls to take to the streets before conditions are ripe.

Tell them clearly: the target is the regime, not the nation, culture, or people of Iran.

Include regime insiders in this messaging, focusing on rank-and-file security forces, the regular military (Artesh), and yes, even IRGC leadership. They will receive the message. Some may act on it.

Be honest about what is coming: that breaking this regime will mean severe economic hardship, power disruptions, and scarcity, possibly even water shortages. Pair that honesty with a credible, binding commitment to a brighter future: a detailed blueprint for immediate relief and reconstruction, asset unfreezing, and re-integration into the global economy once the regime falls.

And lastly, assure them that Iran and Iranians will control their own fate, politically and economically.

I don’t consider myself naïve. This will be difficult. I was a specialist on Iran at the CIA for several decades. I saw both the worst and the best of Iran and Iranians. But the Iranian people (and the world) deserve more than this regime has to offer. Let’s give them (and us) that chance.

Prepare the ground, align the message, then execute.

item.title: Not since 9/11 has the UK faced such a security crisis – and threat to our liberal principles | Gaby Hinsliff
item.description:
The combination of Iranian, Russian and Chinese aggression is deeply worrying: just how much more concerned about security should the country be?

The first time the window-rattling roar of a B-1 bomber woke me up this summer, I thought for one crazed second we were under attack. By the second time, I’d learned to recognise the sound of US planes taking off from their base at RAF Fairford for what it was: a reminder that although Britain wants no part in this war with Iran, we cannot quite escape the consequences.

We’ll feel them at the petrol pump, or in the supermarket this autumn, or in this winter’s heating bills. But living under the flight path adds an extra edge to it. The skies finally fell silent last week, but only because the bombers have been hastily summoned home after an alleged terrorist plot to attack Fairford, in which (according to the prime minister) there are “strong indications that Iran played a part”. If Fairford is now a target of war, did that threat disappear when the Americans did? Nobody knows.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

item.title: The Guardian view on Ethiopia’s return to conflict: civilian catastrophe and a spiralling regional polycrisis | Editorial
item.description:
The escalating violence reflects deep domestic rifts – but is fuelled by broader geopolitical power games

When the Nobel peace laureate is announced on Friday, the committee will be hoping that its choice ages better than 2019’s. Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, won the prize for ending the 20-year border conflict with neighbouring Eritrea – signing a peace agreement with President Isaias Afwerki. A year later, their new relationship facilitated a war with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) that killed as many as 600,000 people, displaced millions more, led to atrocities by both sides, and pushed Tigrayans into famine.

Both sides bear responsibility for failing to properly implement the deal that ended that conflict in 2022, and the African Union and US did little to ensure that a piece of paper became a durable settlement. Now violence has resurged in northern Ethiopia, and old foes are forming bizarre new pacts. Last month, seven Ethiopian regional groups announced an “Alliance for Survival” to remove the federal government. Mr Abiy’s coalition is held together by his patronage, but so far may be faring better than his rivals, united solely by shared loathing of him and riven by deep disputes. The TPLF, which controls Tigray, has previously battled the Fano militia of Amhara, and their territorial dispute endures. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea – previously accused of atrocities against Tigrayan civilians – of backing the rebel alliance. Despite Asmara’s denials, there are multiple reports of Eritrean troops in Tigray.

2027: The Ukraine winter we prayed wouldn't come
item.description:
Let’s imagine a bit of “future history” in Ukraine.

It is February 2027. The Ukrainian winter has been unusually cold, and Russian air strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, transportation grid, and communications networks have been increasingly destructive. Ukraine has no effective defenses against massive barrages of Russian missiles, glide bombs, and jet-powered drones, as Russian President Vladimir Putin seeks both to cripple Ukraine’s ability to field an effective military and to break its will to continue fighting.

Lacking heat, water, and electricity, millions of Ukrainians are fleeing Kyiv and other major cities. Western embassies are temporarily relocating from the capital to safer environs. Russian attacks on data centers and Starlink terminals begin to erode Ukraine’s battlefield targeting and communications, jeopardizing its prospects for holding the last two “fortress cities” in the Donbas region once warmer weather allows ground combat to intensify.

Amid growing fears of starvation and hypothermia, international aid organizations declare a humanitarian crisis in Ukraine. Western media accuse Putin of perpetrating crimes against humanity, and NATO allies press Washington for action, worried that their vision of Ukraine as an enduring “steel porcupine,” armed to the teeth against Russian aggression for decades to come, looks increasingly illusory. The U.S. Congress – now controlled by Democrats following their resounding victories in mid-term elections – demands that Trump stop Russian attacks and rally the NATO alliance around defense of Ukraine.

Trump’s menu of diplomatic options to halt or deter Russia looks disturbingly thin, however. Neither the threat of new economic sanctions nor the lure of new business deals has dented Putin’s opposition to a provisional ceasefire arrangement. Moscow continues to insist that no ceasefire is possible absent a broader peace settlement that addresses key political and security issues in Ukraine and ends NATO enlargement. But there is little appetite in Washington or Europe for negotiating with Russia over such matters, particularly in the midst of an ongoing humanitarian crisis in Ukraine.

The military menu looks similarly unappetizing. Western stockpiles of Patriot air defense missiles have all but disappeared, depleted by years of war in Ukraine and many months of intense missile combat with Iran. New production will take years to meet Ukraine’s needs. Ukraine’s small fleet of F-16 fighter aircraft – perhaps its most effective defense against jet-powered drones – has been largely grounded by maintenance woes, and Europe worries that large-scale transfers of additional fighter aircraft to Ukraine could leave NATO uncomfortably vulnerable should war erupt with Russia.

Given the paucity of alternatives, Western planners gravitate toward a high-risk “escalate to de-escalate” strategy. Some call for imposing a “no- fly zone,” using NATO combat air patrols over Ukrainian airspace to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones and cruise missiles. Not wanting to risk direct combat in Ukraine, however, NATO ultimately decides to position ground and naval forces around the land and maritime borders of Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave, warning Moscow that continuing its efforts to deprive Ukraine of heat, electricity, and other vital supplies will produce a corresponding squeeze of Kaliningrad’s population.

Russia and the West soon find themselves in a genuine military crisis. Moscow reiterates its warning that it will respond to a blockade of Kaliningrad with its full arsenal of armaments, including nuclear weapons. In turn, the United States and NATO effectively dare Russia to fire the first shot against Western forces threatening Russia’s access to Kaliningrad through Lithuania and the Baltic Sea.

Such a scenario is far from inevitable. Lamentably, however, it is becoming not only imaginable but increasingly likely, as U.S.-mediated peace talks stall and Russia becomes convinced that the Trump administration has no ability – and Europe has no desire – to orchestrate a settlement that addresses Russia’s core concerns anytime soon.

What might Team Trump do to reduce the odds of such dangerous developments? The most effective approach would also be the most unlikely under present circumstances: to broaden the scope of its negotiations with Moscow to include talks on European security issues beyond Ukraine. Such talks would consider new mechanisms for crisis management and risk reduction with Russia, confidence- and security-building measures, and conventional and nuclear arms control. The prospect of new accords on matters critical to Russian security would provide Putin with a significant incentive to soften his demands over Ukraine.

Nonetheless, U.S. officials have so far not pursued this course, and key European leaders have ruled it out.

Short of formal talks,Trump could take two steps that might reduce the risks of a future crisis. The first would be to recognize that the “escalate to de-escalate” strategy – which the West has pursued in various forms since early in this war – has consistently led to Russian counter-escalation rather than concessions. Moscow insists that its increasingly brutal air campaign is a response to Ukraine’s campaign of long-range drone attacks on Russian energy and commercial targets, and it has hardened its negotiating demands as Ukrainian attacks have continued.

Given that Kyiv has not achieved its goals (witness the meager impact of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s proclaimed “Forty-Day Influence Campaign” on Russian decision-making), while providing Putin with a ready justification for intensifying Russian air strikes, it makes little sense for the United States to continue enabling Ukrainian long-range strikes with critical targeting data.

The second would be to open what is often termed a “back channel” with Moscow: a private, informal dialogue between a trusted Trump envoy and a Kremlin designee aimed at clarifying each side’s redlines and discussing in advance how to avoid or manage the kinds of crises that might emerge between Washington and Moscow in the coming months and years.

In view of the robust media attention that White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attract every time they meet with Putin or their Russian counterpart, Kirill Dmitriev, they are ill-suited to play such a discreet role. The publicity surrounding CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s recent visit to Moscow underscores how difficult it is for prominent American officials to conduct such talks in secret. However, Trump certainly has access to experienced but lower-profile American experts well suited to perform this role.

Sooner or later, Washington and Moscow will have to discuss these matters, whether the Ukraine war ends at the negotiating table or escalates into a larger crisis. The time to start discussing them is now.

item.title: US leaves Iraq: 'Shock and awe' curdles into 'Aw, shucks'
item.description:
The Bunker appears originally at the Project on Government Oversight and is republished here with permission.

The U.S. ended its military campaign in Iraq on September 30, as the final American combat troops based there left the country. Their departure ended 23 years of fitful fighting. They found no weapons of mass destruction, which was the battering ram President George W. Bush and his combative coterie used to scaremonger the U.S to invade in 2003. We captured Saddam Hussein, and the Iraqis hanged him in 2006. We toppled his Ba’athist regime, only to see it replaced with a government that today is riven with next-door Iran’s influence.

It’s important to remember how this war looks from the other end of the telescope. Two weeks before it began, The Bunker asked Air Force General Richard Myers, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, how the Pentagon’s ballyhooed “shock and awe” campaign would unfold. “If asked to go into conflict in Iraq, what you’d like to do is have it be a short conflict,” he responded. “The best way to do that would be to have such a shock on the system that the Iraqi regime would have to assume early on the end was inevitable.”

Well, you know what they say about assume. In fact, a fellow Air Force officer, Colonel Clarence Lollar, spelled it out in 1964, 39 years before Myers used the word to explain why the Iraq war would be short:

"Mister, when you have an important job to do, never assume. When you look at the word, you can see it is made up of three parts — 'ass,' 'u,' and 'me.' When you rely on assumptions, sooner or later it will make an ass of both of us."

Turns out toppling Saddam was only the beginning of a generation-long campaign that cost 4,418 U.S. troops their lives. It will end up costing U.S. taxpayers an estimated $2.9 trillion through 2050, including veterans’ care yet unbilled.

The Bunker spent years reporting on the war, and its spasmodic successes like toppling Baghdad, hunting down Saddam in his “spider hole,” and the jittery calm wrought by “the surge” of U.S. troops into Iraq in 2007. But he also told the stories of those killed, as well as those who killed themselves (and their family). He wrote about the more than 30,000 physically wounded, as well as the roughly 15% of the 1.5 million U.S. troops who served in Iraq who came home mentally maimed. He covered the military’s inadequate, and sometimes fatal, efforts to render aid, even among those trying to deliver it. He reported on the war’s deadly impact on recruiters back home. He wrote about those captured, dead or alive, as they used to say in the Westerns. Not to mention the 3,600 contractors, and perhaps 200,000 Iraqi civilians, killed in the war.

The stories were tough to report, tough to write, and they remain tough to read.

But in the hurly-burly of today’s world, the heroes at the heart of these stories must never be forgotten.

We must remember and honor their sacrifice, even as we ponder its wisdom, given its paltry prize.

Otherwise, it might happen again.

Long overdue, but it must be done right


The same day the U.S. military pulled out of Iraq, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pledged to continue his campaign to shrink the Pentagon’s nearly 1,000-strong corps of generals and admirals by 20% (he’s currently about halfway there). “The media calls that a purge,” he said. “I call it accountability, and long overdue.”

Accountability, of course, is in the eye of the beholder. We here at the Project On Government Oversight have long fought to cut the U.S. military’s senior ranks. “We have more officers than we need — and we're running the risk of creating a military force of bureaucrats rather than warriors,” Executive Director Danielle Brian said … in 1998. The numbers don’t lie: The ranks of generals and admirals, as their share of the entire U.S. military, has grown by 40% since Vietnam.

But the cutting has to be smart. Based on the results of the Iran war — so far — it’s plain that neither Hegseth nor his military high command knows how to wage war smartly. Promoting the right military personnel is just as challenging. Bazookaing brass that displease the boss doesn’t automatically lead to a lighter and, to coin a phrase, lethaler fighting force. Based on Hegseth’s track record, his thinning of the herd is likely to be more about politics and partisanship than proficiency and prowess.

“This is just a less personal version of the purge he’s already been executing since taking office,” Virginia Burger, a Marine veteran now here at POGO’s Center for Defense Information, says. “By announcing he’s cutting the generals by 20%, he has justification for refusing to promote scores of officers without even having to pull their names from [promotion] lists. This just lets him continue to remove senior leaders who are in the strongest positions to oppose him and his actions.”

Air Force 1, Navy 0


The Bunker is leery of drawing bottom-line conclusions from complicated issues. But every once in a while two things happen simultaneously in the national-security space that support such simplicity. While we were away, the Navy awarded Boeing a $20 billion contract to develop a sixth-generation fighter for its aircraft carriers. (Fighter “generations” share technological innovations; sixth-gen fighters will fly further and more stealthily than their predecessors and be able to command drones from their cockpits.)

But this F/A-XX Strike Fighter represents a doubling-down on yesterday’s technology. Bluntly speaking, it means putting planes flown by humans aboard huge sitting ducks that will be prime targets for any future U.S. foe (whether those planes will be launched by steam or electromagnetic catapults, a separate war now underway between the U.S. Navy and the U.S. president, is irrelevant, albeit amusing).

Meanwhile, seven companies are seeking to build a cheaper MQ-9 Reaper. That’s the Air Force drone its top officer calls the “most valuable player” in the U.S. war against Iran. Unfortunately, the service has lost about 25% of its Reapers in the fight. You probably didn’t know that because drones don’t carry pilots and therefore no U.S. troops died in the drones’ destruction. One of the companies wants to produce Reaper replacements for about one-third the cost of the $30 million Reaper.

This striking contrast needs to be kept in perspective. After all, the Navy is buying drones, and the Air Force is buying its own fleet of sixth-generation fighters. In fact, it’s buying them from Boeing. Letting Boeing build the Navy’s newest fighter, as well as the Air Force’s F-47 (its designation honoring you-know-who, if not strictly speaking, in a “Let’s go, Brandon” kind of way) gives some military-aviation geeks the heebie-jeebies. “Incredulity was the main public reaction, for understandable reasons,” veteran defense-aerospace scribe Bill Sweetman noted. That’s because it means “most unattractively, putting all the Pentagon’s fighter-development eggs in one basket.” Others fear the Navy contract award gives Boeing a “monopoly” and “stranglehold” on U.S. fighter development and production for the next generation, or more.

That lack of competition should make taxpayers nervous. After all, Lockheed is the only company producing the troubled fifth-generation F-35 for the Air Force, Navy, and Marines.

But for the moment, let’s simply cheer the Air Force’s fledgling push to fly and fight more cheaply.

Pentagon mum on Iran war’s cost


The Congressional Budget Office is a nonpartisan bean-counting shop that has spent more than a half-century double-checking the sometimes dubious arithmetic of the Executive Branch. It works, as its name makes clear, for Congress. Congress, in turn, works for us — the American people who pay taxes to fund this government. So it’s beyond disconcerting that the Pentagon recently stiff-armed the CBO after the agency asked the U.S. military about the cost of the war in Iran (the CBO estimated that the war cost U.S. taxpayers $38 billion through August 1).

“To estimate DoD's costs, CBO relied on government databases and public reports because DoD did not respond to CBO's requests for information,” the CBO said in a September 15 report. “As a result, CBO's estimates are subject to considerable uncertainty.”

Gobsmacking.

Here we have a war unilaterally launched by President Donald Trump and waged by a Pentagon that has rarely briefed what’s left of the Defense Department press corps on its progress. Now they’re declining to tell the CBO how much they’re spending on it.

Back in the good ol’ days MIA meant “missing in action.” In the current environment it means “mission isn’t auditable.”

Here’s what has caught The Bunker's eye recently

→ Not so fast, admirals…

Mystery drones have been spotted over the key U.S. military base on Diego Garcia in the middle of the Indian Ocean, The War Zone’s Howard Altman reported August 10.

→ Where there’s a will, there’s a weigh

The Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency is using new analytical tools to try to measure a foreign military’s will to fight, Breaking Defense’s Lee Ferran reported September 30.

→ The non-Archie Bunker

Trump administration officials said they were unaware of plans to convert the president’s proposed triumphal arch into a military complex, after Trump announced plans to put snipers, drones, and ammunition at the site, the Washington Post’s Dan Diamond reported September 29.

item.title: Anduril building US submarines? It's not the craziest idea.
item.description:
President Donald Trump traveled to Baltimore this week to announce a $7 billion deal with the defense tech firm Anduril to build autonomous submarines as well as components for the Navy’s Virginia-class attack submarines. When fully implemented, the plan is expected to revitalize the Sparrows Point area of the city that once employed nearly 30,000 people at a steel mill and shipyard run by Bethlehem Steel.

The announcement has been met with mixed reactions. A major point of concern seems to be Anduril’s expansion into traditional defense contracts. The company was established in 2017 and has focused on building autonomous drones and sea vehicles and developing AI-enabled software to operate them. American submarines are currently built by General Dynamics and Huntington Ingalls Industries.

The announcement has raised some eyebrows considering Anduril’s founder Palmer Lucky’s recent appointment as a co-lead, along with Elon Musk and Newt Gingrich, on a Pentagon study about AI-powered weapons and the future of warfare. It remains to be seen how Anduril, a company that has so far specialized in small drones will fare building components like torpedo tubes for crewed vessels, to say nothing of scaling up to eventually build hull sections. The company will undoubtedly face a steep learning curve as it expands into more traditional defense contracts.

One of the biggest challenges the company will face will be the same workforce issues plaguing its existing counterparts. The Government Accountability Office reported last year that the shipbuilding industrial base needs 174,000 new workers in the next decade to keep pace with the Navy’s needs. Anduril’s expansion will only add to those workforce demands.

But such concerns should be tempered a bit considering the current state of American shipbuilding and years of ineffective defense policies.

The U.S. Navy has floundered in nearly every effort to develop a major new shipbuilding program in this century. The Zumwalt-class destroyer, Littoral Combat Ship, and the Constellation-class program are all complete failures. The USS Ford entered active service years behind schedule and billions over budget and now the sailors serving aboard the aircraft carrier can’t even rely on the ship’s toilets to flush.

Politicians and Navy officials have decried the woeful state of the submarine industrial base for years. Calls for greater investment to increase the production rate of submarines have become a regular feature of defense budget debates. In 2015, Navy leaders discussed the possibility of expanding attack submarine production from two to three boats each year. Members of Congress added $250 million to strengthen the submarine industrial base in 2018. By 2024, $3.3 billion in “critical” investments were made for the same purpose.

For all of those investments, the production rate for attack submarines has gone from two per year in 2015 to 1.3 in 2026. Falling submarine production rates are particularly problematic at the moment because demand is increasing. The AUKUS deal between the U.S., United Kingdom, and Australia would see the latter country receive three Virginia-class submarines in the coming years.

Concerns about crony capitalism and potential conflicts of interest when it comes to Anduril’s Baltimore deal are real, but so is the fact that, despite investing billions of dollars to improve the submarine construction problem, it has only gotten worse. To judge from some of the breathless coverage of the deal, a casual reader would think this is the first time a politician has ever steered a defense contract to a campaign donor. In this particular case, it should be noted that the Trump administration inked a deal where the principal economic beneficiary is a state that voted for Kamala Harris by nearly 30 points in 2024.

In an ideal world, the American people would not need things like a submarine. In a better world, national security policymakers would make every decision with military effectiveness as their primary concern. But in the real world of 2026, this plan might just be the best option to meet America’s future security needs.

How Ukraine’s Ground Robots Are Changing the Battlefield
item.description:
Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian military effort to repel Russian forces in the Donbas, has done much more than push back Moscow’s offensive in the region. The operation is credited with the liberation of dozens of square miles of once Russian held territory because of its mastermind use of drones and robotics on the battlefield. The operation has also ignited a firestorm of debate over the future of war and the human role. What follows is independent analysis of Operation Vivaldi by two Cipher Brief contributors who are actively engaged in the region.

INDEPENDENT ANALYSIS – Some Western commentators have suggested that Ukraine’s successful limited counteroffensive, Operation Vivaldi, by the 3rd Army Corps (3AC) has demonstrated the continued relevance of human maneuver in the face of drone technology, downplaying the ascendancy of drone warfare. In fact, Operation Vivaldi demonstrates just the opposite: the inexorable erosion of the usefulness of humans in direct contact with the enemy.

While isolated videos on social media may be found of direct fires exchanged between small elements of humans during the ongoing counteroffensive, the bulk of OSINT footage, as well as comments from Ukrainian commanders and soldiers, indicates that a new, systematic doctrine for the use of UGVs (unmanned ground vehicles) has been critical to operational success, and that humans generally advance only into lower-risk areas in the wake of waves of ground-drone advances.

The key to this doctrine is a fusion of classic American warfighting principles (taught to Ukrainians) with new tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), together with a recognition of the changing spatial dimensions of modern warfare. In Operation Vivaldi, the aforementioned TTPs notably included the use of air-dropped UGVs to strike Russian positions, sow chaos behind enemy lines, take and hold ground, and clear lanes through minefields ahead of human advances.

According to “Darwin,” commander of the 2nd Mechanized Battalion of the 3AC, Russian soldiers and drones were suppressed by artillery, strike drones, and electronic warfare in order to prevent them from noticing night flights of repurposed heavy bomber drones carrying UGVs up to 19 kilometers deep into Russian lines. Some air-dropped UGVs with bombs struck Russian positions, while other UGVs with small arms would take and hold ground, sometimes killing and sometimes capturing the enemy in the process. Only then would humans incrementally advance: “We go forward, making a defense line, then waiting until artillery, flying drones and robots do their work, and then go in again.”

His men still only did this in small groups, with no restoration of large simultaneous human maneuver: “If before we moved with big battalion groups with mechanized forces, now we should use only small groups because of drones.” While this new pattern is currently only reported in use by 3AC, Darwin “said his corps was already teaching it to other brigades,” but noted that it required “a command structure ‘qualified enough as we are’ to run an operation with that many moving parts.”

But Ukraine still needed to degrade Russian operations before attempting to advance. Besides utilizing kinetic strikes, Ukrainian forces also deployed an electronic warfare “curtain” over parts of the battlefield, masking some Ukrainian movements and preventing Russian reconnaissance drones from operating. According to the Third Army Corps, its comprehensive “Defensive Dome” eliminated around 20,000 Russian drones during the operation, including via the use of interceptor drones, freeing Ukrainian armor to conduct mechanized assaults.

“Makar,” commander of the UGV unit “NG13” of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade of the 3AC, says that air-dropped UGVs were used for months by his unit as “part of a systematic approach to sabotage operations, as such missions are aimed at eliminating the enemy deep behind their lines and in hideouts, capturing enemy pilots, disrupting logistics, and so on.” While the air-dropping technique itself may be a temporary novelty, the systematic large-scale use of UGVs ahead of humans may lead to a situation that he says “changes the rules of war.”

Makar continues: “We are developing a global doctrine for the use of UGVs... by the end of 2026, we’ll carry out a number of crazy operations the world... can’t even imagine are possible.” Regarding the military structure required, he mentions “strong coordination between the units we work with on these missions” and “the work of the workshop, planning group, command staff, and operators on duty.” He also notes the particular usefulness of UGVs--typically equipped with Starlink, hard to notice by the enemy, and not limited by station time like unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs)--in enemy-held areas “where we have limited observation, limited FPV range, restricted operating distances, or where the enemy has strong air defense teams.”

Russian infantry has seen some success with infiltration tactics, able to slip through gaps in the thin Ukrainian lines singly or in pairs, due to the Russian tolerance for horrific casualties among such drone fodder.

Ukrainian UGVs, which need not be conserved like humans, are now performing similar infiltration missions against the Russians, but at even greater depth and sowing even greater disruption. “A UGV armed with a machine gun is probably more intimidating than an infantryman in many situations,” Obi, a soldier from Ukraine’s 3rd Special Operations Regiment, told the authors.

Makar described how in one episode, a single UGV caused disproportionate chaos: “They were freaking out over the radio, ‘A toy car flew in, then drove around, and then exploded...’ Well, their command doesn’t believe them, all hell breaks loose, and movement along that logistics route is immediately banned. All positions were placed on full combat alert... There were many times when they said, ‘No, we won’t go there because it’s unclear what’s going on there,’ and so on.” In another episode, “a single small UGV, airdropped some distance away, eliminated one enemy soldier and as a result, a full-scale enemy assault they’d been planning for days, if not weeks, was called off.”

Finally, Makar specifically refers to UGVs as a kind of replacement for infantry, saying: “Paratroopers used to drop from planes. Now UGVs are dropped from heavy bombers... I would like to address all the commanders... Emphasize ground robotic complexes... because robots don’t bleed, and human life is priceless.” Still, although they aren’t priceless like humans, drones need protection too: during Operation Vivaldi, relatively expendable UAVs were used to scout ahead of and escort UGVs.

Dmytro, a soldier with Ukraine’s Third Separate Assault Brigade, told the authors that drones and ground robots play a key role in supporting the infantry and also remove humans from some of the most dangerous tasks. “There are also many strike ground robots that drive in and destroy enemy shelters, killing the personnel inside,” he said. Some robots are meant to engage in assault operations, while others are sent behind enemy lines to conduct ambushes.

Additionally, as Ukrainian infantry and drone operators move forward, ground robots handle much of the logistics. “Ground robots make all kinds of deliveries to positions, including supplies for drone crews,” said Dmytro. “They deliver ammunition to artillery positions and supplies to the front line, and they carry out many evacuations.” In fact, 80% of tactical logistics and 90% of casualty evacuations during Operation Vivaldi were done by UGVs.

Former American soldier “Jackie,” who volunteered to serve with and advise 3AC, emphasizes that the American style of warfighting and command culture is critical to the integration of the emerging doctrine and new technologies seen in Operation Vivaldi.

“That’s been my job primarily is installing Western mission command trust and initiative.” Such concepts are embraced by 3AC, but don’t work at all for Russians: “It wouldn’t matter if I gave [them] a perfect lecture on Western Mission Command because they’re asking their guys to go die for nothing constantly... you can’t have initiative and trust in that environment... they misreport and they lie all the time.”

The effective military culture together with scaled drone use has resulted in three Russian field armies being pushed back by the much smaller 3AC, which consistently achieves an astonishingly favorable exchange ratio of 20:1 against the Russians (a claim backed up by OSINT as well as Ukraine’s battle “points” awarded according to provable kills, in which 3AC is usually leading when compared to other Ukrainian units).

Jackie points out, however, that Ukrainians have advanced past legacy doctrine and that Western commanders and planners need a feedback loop with people on the ground to keep up with what’s happening: “We’ve all been doing this for four and a half years. We are super experienced now. The operational planners who did this are elite. Sometimes you get a graduate of some war college somewhere with two pumps in the Middle East that says ‘I know everything about war and the Ukrainians should do this and that’... if you want to learn something by the way you actually have to participate in this fight. And I’m trying to constantly give out calls to Western forces... to come over here and do some work with us.”

“The theory of battle for the Ukrainians is really good. So they have a strategic deep strike campaign that’s punishing the Russian economy. At the operational level we have the midstrike campaign” targeting Russian logistics, “forcing them to have to vacate” their forward positions due to the extension of the gray zone. He adds: “The ground game is really important. If we lose the fortress belt, there will not be time for the midstrike campaign to pull Russians back. There will not be time to continue to do damage on the deep strike campaign and make the political actors in Russia pay.”

One new element of Ukrainian doctrine Jackie mentions is the need for standoff. 3AC maintains “control of ground space that enables us to continue to intercept Russian drones overhead. Russians are not able to get rocket artillery and other mass fires in range of the city of Izium.”

He says, “There is no contact line. There’s like a contact zone and that zone is 30 km across.” He emphasizes that this contact zone or “gray zone” is not a confused or messy jumble on the ground; Ukrainian commanders know where their men are positioned. But in this zone, human maneuver and logistics are severely constrained.

Dmytro said that Ukrainian forces attempted to bypass wooded areas and cut off Russian logistics, instead of sending infantry first. Ukrainian forces also continued shooting down the larger drones the Russians were using for resupply, which had a crippling effect on morale. “The enemy infantry begins to feel that no one needs them and that no help or support is coming,” he said. “Their morale becomes very low, and we make progress. Then they surrender or start fleeing.”

The principle behind the aforementioned infiltration tactics applies also to the enemy’s defense, as Jackie explains: “Where there’s just Russians all over the place that nobody cares about, and clearing them out is a pain... Driving a column across the gray zone is not an option to make an assault. That’s definitely not what we did for Vivaldi. So we had the ground drones on logistics, but also attack ground drones that were being air dropped behind the Russian line and then isolating and either fixing or destroying in many cases those isolated pockets of Russians on defense.”

UGVs are also more effective in this role than UAVs because “The Russians are going to have to fight that drone for a period of time. They’re going to have to resource Russian effectors to support the Russian fight against that drone. So in that local area this is creating ... massive chaos for whatever company’s area that drone got dropped into... they’re going to totally miss the infantry assault that’s actually approaching and being shaped towards them... some of those ground drop drones were technically like objectives for assault units to go and support... It gives everybody a lot of confidence on the assault to know that we already have a friendly force in the local area and so everybody gets moving faster as well.”

Jackie says that the soldier’s primary weapon is becoming the drone, and his pistol (secondary weapon) is being replaced by the shotgun for defensive use against drones. Yet he concedes that “there’s only one job in the military and that’s infantry. Nothing has changed about that. For all the drones... [What matters is] the ground game right in front of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk with those infantrymen.” But clearly, from all the other quotes above, we can gather that the nature of the infantryman’s work is rapidly transforming into something entirely different from closing with and destroying other infantry with rifle fire and grenades.Therefore Jackie’s point is taken to be that humans and the ground they occupy remain the ultimate tactical objective of the drones that increasingly occupy the buffer zone between them and the enemy’s forward line of humans.

Applying this notion back to the larger operational concept, we can say that combined unmanned-systems warfare, together with advanced mission command and a proper military culture based on initiative and trust, can allow unmanned systems to maneuver through the enemy’s tactical depth before human forces ever advance into the resultant pre-cleared areas.

Take it from the 3rd Army Corps: “Infantry wins wars, but we protect our infantry, which is why the robots go to the enemy first."

For deeper dives from Xen, you can follow him on X, Substack, or his personal site.

item.title: The Next Drone Won't Have a Radio Link, Our Intelligence Enterprise Needs to Plan for That Now
item.description:
On the last day of the 2026 World Cup, NORAD F-16s fired flares over northern New Jersey to warn off civilian pilots who had flown into restricted airspace. During the tournament, federal agencies seized more than 700 drones across 11 host cities. The counter-drone effort worked.

That's what worries me.

In less than two years, Los Angeles will open the 2028 Olympic Games, a National Special Security Event spread across dozens of venues followed weeks later by the Paralympics. The threat there won't be the one we just beat, and this summer's solutions won't be the ones we need.

I've seen this before. From 2010 to 2013 I ran the Army's Rapid Equipping Force in the middle of the counter-IED fight. Congress authorized roughly $21 billion for JIEDDO, and we spent nearly $50 billion more on MRAPs. We still lost the adaptation race. The enemy learned and changed faster than our institutions could. Drones have the same traits that made IEDs so hard to beat: cheap dual-use parts, know-how that spreads through informal networks, and changes that cost the adversary almost nothing. Drones are IEDs that fly.

The next drone won't have a radio link

We don't lack counter-drone technology. But every answer we field starts a clock; someone is already building the counter. In Ukraine and the Gulf, autonomous navigation that doesn't need GPS is maturing quickly. One operator can run a swarm, and AI handles terminal guidance. Most counter-drone systems fielded today detect the radio link between drone and operator, and jam it. The drones that matter in 2028 may not have one.

When the sensor at the venue can't hear the drone, the warning has to come from before launch. Left of launch is intelligence.

Weak signals become capabilities before we see them

The drone threat rarely announces itself. During the battle for Mosul in 2016 and 2017, ISIS dropped small munitions from commercial quadcopters. In 2024, fiber-optic drones appeared in Ukraine as a workaround to jamming and quickly became widespread. In June 2025, Ukraine smuggled more than 100 small drones into Russia hidden in trucks, flew them over commercial mobile networks with open-source autopilot software, and struck strategic bomber bases as far away as Siberia. It was built from commercial parts and networks. The capability was the combination.

The same thing is happening here, in plain sight. A small startup has built software that keeps data moving when networks fail, uses AI agents to fuse that data and recommend actions, and ships new features every week. It's built for logistics. Pair it with an off-the-shelf mesh radio sold for drones; vendors say some can cover thousands of square miles from altitude. In a matter of months, a small team could field a jam-resistant, AI-assisted network of drones and sensors that no requirement anticipated and no threat library lists.

Nothing about either piece is a threat. That's the problem. We catalog platforms; the threat emerges in the combinations. And the expertise to put them together is for hire. This month, a Ukrainian air defense officer offered me his team's combat experience on LinkedIn.

Intelligence is more than threat warning

Our intelligence enterprise tends to treat counter-drone support as a threat function: who is flying, what they intend, what is coming. That job matters, but it's one of three.

The second job is awareness. Near a stadium or a base, most drones are flown by hobbyists, photographers, delivery services or people who never checked the rules. The hard problem is finding the one that matters in a crowded sky. That takes a picture of normal: Remote ID, FAA authorizations, event credentials, known commercial traffic. Most of that data sits outside intelligence channels, with the FAA, commercial operators, and state and local agencies that gained their own counter-drone authority on July 1 under the SAFER SKIES Act. The fusion model has to be built with these partners, not around them.

The third job is adaptation. Every drone we recover tells us how the adversary is changing: firmware, components, frequencies, supply chains. That knowledge has to reach the people building countermeasures and the units that will face the same drone next week. When Gen. Stanley McChrystal's task force in Iraq tied intelligence to operations, it went from about 18 raids a month in 2004 to about 300 a month by 2006. Not with better equipment, but because every completed cycle made the next one faster.

One threat, one learning loop

It's tempting to treat Los Angeles as a homeland security problem and the Gulf as a warfighting problem. The drone doesn't care. The same parts, tactics and know-how reach forward bases, stateside installations and crowded stadiums at the same time. Northern Command couldn't determine who flew several drones over a strategic U.S. installation after the Iran campaign began this year.

That cuts both ways. What we exploit from a drone downed overseas is the earliest warning Los Angeles will get. What we test at stadiums at home, in real conditions, strengthens the force overseas. JIATF 401 convenes DHS, the FBI, the FAA and dozens of other federal organizations; its director, Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, puts it plainly: "Nobody can solve this problem alone." Intelligence has to be the engine that makes that connection worth having.

Two clocks, one collision point

Our planning runs on a deliberate, gated clock: fund, test, buy, then freeze the configuration so people can train on it. The adversary's clock has no freeze date. State actors are patient: they watch our events, probe our installations and study our playbook. Extremists and lone actors copy what works overseas, hide among careless flyers and can change tactics up to the day they act. Whatever becomes cheap and proven overseas in early 2028 will be available to them in July 2028.

The collision point is our freeze date. Whatever they adopt after it, we meet unrehearsed.

The answer: test continuously through 2027 at real events, buy fast in early 2028, and never fully freeze. Keep money, authority and software update paths open so something can still change in the final 90 days.

Intelligence has to unfreeze the plan

Only intelligence can create the pressure to reopen a plan that has been funded, tested and trained on. Program managers have every incentive not to, and operators rarely get the chance. The intelligence community should schedule those assessments now, tied to the plan's decision points:

  • a threat baseline today
  • a reassessment after every 2027 test and every real incident
  • a formal assessment before we buy
  • a final one inside the last 90 days

Each should answer one question: what has changed that should change the plan?

Sometimes the answer will be "nothing." The system has to be ready for the times it's "a lot." That means flexible funding that portfolio managers can move as the threat moves, and a Congress willing to let them.

In Afghanistan, when the enemy adapted faster than we did, soldiers and allies paid for the delay. We know the date of the next test. Build for the threat we'll face in 2028, not the one we just beat.

Pete Newell is the CEO of BMNT and a former director of the Army's Rapid Equipping Force.

item.title: The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash
item.description:
Moscow’s imperialist strongman believes decadent European democracies can be cowed. Our job is to prove him wrong

Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own. While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine. Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.

In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology. He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”. West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (eg something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe.

item.title: Why Saudi Arabia has returned to war in Yemen
item.description:
When Ansar Allah—commonly referred to as the Houthis—seized Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandab Strait on September 10, 2026, they appeared to gain the upper hand in Yemen’s long-running conflict. However, in early October Saudi-backed government forces began to retake some of the captured territory and Saudi Arabia launched a punishing assault on Houthi positions from the air. France, Pakistan, and the United States have all sent personnel to help the kingdom counter the Houthi offensive.

Outside the region, some have portrayed the Houthi offensive as another theater within the broader US-Israeli war on Iran. However, this broader regional war is separate from the war in Yemen, which can be traced back to the Houthi takeover of Yemen’s capital Sanaa in September 2014 and the decision by neighboring Saudi Arabia to launch a coalition to oust them in March 2015.

While the Houthis are certainly allied with Iran and benefit from the weapons and support that Tehran has covertly provided them since at least 2009, they have their own agenda: to consolidate their control over Yemen. They would pursue this political objective even if Washington and Tehran somehow agreed to end the war that Trump rashly launched. Still, their recent decision to escalate does reflect the sense of momentum produced by Iran’s success in withstanding American and Israeli attacks. Thus, even as these two conflicts are distinct, the Iran war is both exacerbating and heightening the effects of the violence in Yemen.

The Houthis’ Red Sea offensive


The catalyst for the latest round of violence came on July 13, 2026, when an Iranian civilian plane—carrying a Houthi delegation that had attended the funeral of Iran’s assassinated Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei—returned to Yemen. When the plane attempted to land at Sanaa International Airport, the runway was bombed. Yemen’s internationally recognized government—under the leadership of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC)—took responsibility for the attack, while the Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, which supports the PLC. As a result of the attack, the plane was forced to land in Houthi-controlled Hodeidah. On July 20, the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi Arabia, targeting oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab Strait in retaliation for its attacks and ongoing restrictions on Houthi-controlled territory. The Houthis subsequently targeted Saudi petroleum facilities and oil tankers in the Red Sea.

The attack on Sanaa Airport officially ended the truce that had largely held between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since April 2022.

The attack on Sanaa Airport officially ended the truce that had largely held between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since April 2022. Even before this incident, however, the Houthis appeared to have already been preparing for a return to conflict, mobilizing their fighters and moving materiel into position. In a June 16, 2026, speech, the Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi announced that the group was ready for combat and called for official and grassroots action to end what he described as more than 11 years of Saudi aggression and blockade.

The speech shifted the Houthis’ narrative away from their support for Palestinians, which had become central to the group’s domestic legitimacy in the context of Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza since October 7, 2023. In subsequent months, as the Houthis began striking Israeli ships in the Red Sea in retaliation for their violence against Palestinians, their credibility at home substantially increased, helping paper over their repression and failure to improve the daily lives of Yemenis under their control. The Houthis’ support for Palestine also drove recruitment and raised their international profile. Yet the group also paid for its solidarity with Palestinians, with the United States and Israel hitting Houthi areas with deadly air strikes. In August 2025, Israel assassinated several Houthi cabinet ministers, including the prime minister. Following Netanyahu’s stated commitment to a ceasefire in Gaza in October 2025, the Houthis signaled a pause in their campaign against Israel. Despite Israel’s daily violations of said ceasefire, the Houthis have limited their attacks on Israel, an indication that the group may wish to avoid returning to open conflict with Tel Aviv. Instead, the Houthis shifted focus to Riyadh’s restrictions on their airspace and seaports, as well as Saudi support for the various competing groups that oppose Houthi rule.

The Houthi resurgence


Over the past four years, the Houthis have improved their military capabilities. Increasingly, they can manufacture weapons inside Yemen, although a network of providers, including Iran, continues to provide the raw materials and other components they need. Analysts have claimed that the Houthis have been bringing in large shipments of military material, equipment, and weapons. There are also reports that they have used Claude, Anthropic’s AI tool, to develop guided weapons. As early as 2017, the Houthis experimented with the use of a drone boat, and in the years since have remained at the cutting edge in terms of their use of emerging technologies to threaten adversaries with far more resources and firepower.

The Houthis’ ability to swiftly seize the Red Sea coast from forces loyal to the PLC was further facilitated by the withdrawal of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) from Yemen in January 2026 under pressure from Saudi Arabia. Until early 2026, the UAE provided significant assistance to Yemen’s southern secessionist movement, led by the Southern Transitional Council (STC). The chairman of the STC, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, was also a member of the PLC. However, in December 2025, STC forces suddenly took large swathes of territory in eastern Yemen, which included areas along the Saudi border in the provinces of Hadramawt and al-Mahra. Saudi Arabia responded quickly, bombing Emirati ships transporting weapons to the STC and insisting that the UAE fully withdraw from Yemen. Under Saudi pressure, the STC leadership announced the dissolution of the group, while al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE. The PLC rescinded al-Zubaidi’s membership of the council along with another STC ally, the former governor of Hadramawt, replacing them with two new figures. Yet Saudi Arabia’s attempt to quash the STC hardly quelled demands for southern independence. Instead, it appeared to alienate separatists who previously supported the PLC in the hopes that by doing so, it would lead to an independent southern Yemen.

The PLC’s initial inability to repel the Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast in the current conflict—even with Saudi backing—was seen as a sign of the ruling government’s overall ineffectiveness.

The PLC, in turn, owes much of its own rise to power to Saudi Arabia. After the Arab Spring protests forced President Ali Abdullah Saleh to step down and end his more than 33-year rule over Yemen in 2012, Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi led the internationally recognized government that replaced him, initially with Saudi support. What was meant to be a two-year interim position for Hadi, however, turned into ten. His rule finally ended when Saudi Arabia withdrew its backing and transferred authority to the PLC. The PLC initially comprised eight men, four aligned primarily with Saudi Arabia and four with the UAE.

These dynamics created deep internal divisions in the PLC, which has also been accused of corruption and an inability to improve the quality of life for the population under its authority. Some Yemeni critics have called for reforms to make the PLC more accountable and representative of all Yemenis. In response to such criticisms, in January 2025, PLC chairman Rashad al-Alimi announced a crackdown on corruption. Nevertheless, the PLC’s initial inability to repel the Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast in the current conflict—even with Saudi backing—was seen as a sign of the ruling government’s overall ineffectiveness.

Riyadh and the Houthis: What do they want?


Over the course of the Houthis’ war with Saudi-backed forces from 2015 until 2022, the group advanced its military capabilities, largely through covert Iranian support. The turning point in this war came in March 2022, when the Houthis hit Saudi Arabia during the Formula One Saudi Arabian Grand Prix in Jeddah. The attack showed the Houthis were capable of not only deterring tourists and investors from coming to Saudi Arabia but also threatening the success of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitious Vision 2030 plan to transform the kingdom’s economy and society. Only after the attack did Saudi Arabia agree to a two-month United Nations (UN)-brokered truce in April 2022.

By March 2023, Saudis were reportedly eager to find a longer-term agreement to end their costly and ultimately futile involvement in Yemen. Over the next few months, Riyadh engaged in direct talks with the Houthis, mediated by Oman, in pursuit of that goal, resulting in a broader UN-brokered roadmap agreement in December 2023. Under the terms of this agreement, Saudi Arabia would reportedly pay public sector salaries, including in Houthi-held territory, and would ease restrictions on air and seaports. The deal would have also enabled the resumption of oil exports and initiated an inclusive, Yemeni-led political settlement under UN auspices. In effect, the deal would have disempowered the PLC, which depends largely on Saudi support. When the Houthis initiated hostilities against Israel in late 2023—which prompted the US to launch Operation Prosperity Guardian against them in response—the Saudis were notably absent, unwilling to risk a resumption of transborder attacks.

The Houthis’ flight back and forth from Tehran in July 2026 appears to have crossed a red line for the Saudis.

However, the Houthis’ flight back and forth from Tehran in July 2026 appears to have crossed a red line for the Saudis, and Riyadh feared that showing restraint in this case would merely embolden the Houthis further. In the context of the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia relied more heavily on exporting oil through the Red Sea. When the Houthis began targeting Saudi oil infrastructure, Mohammed bin Salman likely believed that the US would intervene to deliver Saudi oil to the global market. However, Trump’s refusal to directly aid the Saudis in their conflict with the Houthis appears to show Washington’s reluctance to reopen a sustained Yemen campaign while heavily committed elsewhere in the region.

Riyadh’s strategic options


At present, Riyadh faces three options: 1) attempt to reverse Houthi gains militarily through continued partnership with the PLC; 2) shift support to the southern separatists in the STC; or 3) renew negotiations with the Houthis in preparation to withdraw from Yemen. Currently, the Saudis appear to be pursuing the first option. Although the US has declined to resume air strikes on Houthi positions, the United Kingdom is refueling Saudi planes over Yemen. France has also announced that it will send troops to the Saudi city of Yanbu to help secure energy sites. Pakistan began sending troops last year, with between 30,000 and 40,000 reportedly deployed to Saudi Arabia, although not to the front lines in Yemen.

Still, the longer-term viability of the PLC remains in question. The fecklessness of the PLC, in contrast to the relative effectiveness of the STC, has prompted some analysts to suggest that Saudi Arabia should switch its support to groups supporting southern secession. Given Saudi concerns about the implications of an independent southern Yemen for its own security, this option seems unlikely, although with the expulsion of the UAE, Saudi Arabia might try to repair relations with the southerners.

That leaves the possibility of the third option. If the current conflict becomes too costly, or if Saudi Arabia feels that it has improved its bargaining position by adequately damaging the Houthis, Riyadh may return to the negotiating table. Saudi Arabia had previously exhibited willingness to negotiate with the Houthis under the UN-brokered agreements. If they decide to do so again, they may agree to a similar deal, wherein they withdraw support for anti-Houthi forces and allow the Houthis to consolidate control. Yet for many inside Yemen who have fled Houthi rule, this option would be a catastrophe. For example, while the UN has reported that all sides in the conflict have used child soldiers, the Houthis do so in significantly higher numbers. They have also detained hundreds of people, targeting those active in Yemen’s once vibrant civil society. The Houthis’ systematic diversion of humanitarian aid is also well documented by human rights groups. In fact, the Houthis’ practice of kidnapping or attacking UN personnel and aid workers—accusing them of serving as spies for Washington or Tel Aviv—has led several humanitarian organizations to stop operating inside Houthi-controlled territory, to devastating effect for the local population.

Nevertheless, the Houthis have demonstrated themselves to be the most capable security force inside Yemen. Despite attacks on them by the central government in the 2000s, seven years of war with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and an air campaign by Israel and the United States, the Houthis appear to have grown stronger. The resumption of attacks against them by foreign countries only reinforces their narrative that they are the sole defenders of Yemen’s sovereignty.

If foreign powers continue to pour fuel onto Yemen’s conflict, it will continue to rage.

From 2015 to 2022, Saudi Arabia tried unsuccessfully to oust the Houthis from Yemen at a high human cost, as their crippling blockade on the country contributed to the deaths of tens of thousands of children. As such, the Saudis could decide to make a deal with the Houthis and withdraw from Yemen. By building a relationship with the Houthis, the Saudis could also gradually make them less dependent on Iran. In this scenario, the Houthis, southern separatists, and other local actors would be left to determine the balance of power within Yemen. Without the excuse of a foreign aggressor, the Houthis would have no one to blame for their inability to provide for the Yemeni people. But if foreign powers continue to pour fuel onto Yemen’s conflict, it will continue to rage. Although UN mediation in Yemen needs an overhaul, the UN could plausibly play a productive role in helping to facilitate dialogue among the Yemeni factions to finally end the conflict.

Unfortunately, Saudi Arabia, with international support, has resumed its futile assault on Yemen. Riyadh apparently believes that diplomacy has failed and previous efforts to appease the Houthis have merely caused their ambitions to expand. The Yemeni population, many of whom are already on the edge of survival, are paying the price.

In Saudi Arabia, a country that is unaccustomed to such fatalities, the death toll is bewilderingly high and likely to prompt a bloody response.

Over the past year, the Gulf has entered a new era of instability that is not temporary and cannot be reversed. This may feel like an overstatement – casualties have been relatively low, after all, compared with Gaza and Iran – but the gradual erosion of peace and security in places such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE has changed the region more dramatically than its leaders would like to acknowledge.

Subterranean Warfare - An Urgent DoW Need Without An Owner
item.description:
The DoW urgently needs to organize its scattered subterranean warfare assets into a single unified organization. Ideally, a Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager (DRPM) for Subterranean Warfare, reporting to the Deputy Secretary of War. (The Department already uses this model for unmanned systems, critical weapons and Golden Dome.) This group would have three portfolios: Subterranean Resilience, Subterranean Sensing and Subterranean Defeat. The office would integrate validated requirements, experimentation, testing, acquisition, and fielding.

Subterranean Resilience

During the 2026 Iran conflict, Iranian ballistic missiles and low-cost drones hit U.S. installations across eight Middle Eastern countries. Hundreds of buildings and structures were damaged or destroyed. The Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain was among the installations hit hard. Iranian weapons damaged one E-3 airborne early-warning aircraft and five KC-135 tankers on the ground in Saudi Arabia. (The official inspector-general report documents the damage.) Despite thousands of successful interceptions, the attacks exposed the vulnerability of concentrated, above-ground assets.

The rapid redeployment of the B-1s from RAF Fairford in the UK after warnings of an Iran-linked threat (reported as a possible drone attack) made the point: unsheltered concentrated high-value aircraft are vulnerable even way outside the theater.

The assumptions the U.S. has made about air superiority, missile defense, aircraft dispersal, building hardening, and the survivability of concentrated forward bases were all flawed. While we were prepared for ballistic missiles and hostile aircraft, drone swarms combined with ballistic missiles saturated and got through our defenses.

Washington’s reaction has been to invest billions of dollars in counter-drone and missile defense systems. Yet public budget documents reveal no comparable effort to put vulnerable aircraft, fuel, command-and-control nodes, and munitions out of harm’s way – sheltered, underground (or in space). (Agile Combat Employment, dispersal, hardening, deception, shelters, and rapid runway repair were never designed for a combined drone and missile onslaught.)

The Pentagon has recognized for decades that underground facilities are among the most effective ways an adversary can blunt U.S. conventional superiority. It described that problem explicitly in 1999. Gaza and Ukraine should have made it abundantly clear.

China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran use underground facilities, dispersal, hardening, and deception to make their own high-value assets harder to find, assess, and disable. We need to underground assets that cannot be quickly replaced: command posts, comms nodes, ammunition, fuel distribution points, repair facilities, key power systems, maintenance spares, and high-value aircraft or drones. The department needs an integrator that coordinates resilience across the Military Departments, Joint Staff, combatant commands, defense agencies, and intelligence community and provides Subterranean Resilience.

However, resilience is only one part of subterranean warfare.

Subterranean Sensing and Defeat

The U.S. needs to know where adversaries' underground facilities are located, and the internal layout of those facilities. Today, these bespoke exquisite systems for tunnel detection, robotic mapping of accessible tunnels, Hard and Deeply Buried Targets (HDBT) characterization, and target defeat are siloed in organizations scattered across the DoW. Most of these systems still require boots on the ground. Once a target is found, Combatant Commands need an integrated system that can characterize and destroy these targets, without first gaining physical access. Today, for the deepest facilities that means bombing from the air. Iran is the case in point.

Background. Iran's route to a nuclear weapon is by enriching uranium. Natural uranium is composed of 0.71% uranium-235 (U235) and it’s only the U235 that is used to build a bomb.

Iran uses centrifuges to separate U235 and increase its concentration (enriching it.) One centrifuge won’t do much, but connecting thousands of centrifuges together into cascades and running them for months can produce pounds of U235.

Iran’s underground nuclear enrichment site at Natanz had well over 10,000 centrifuges installed across dozens of cascades, and their Fordow nuclear enrichment site was built for 16 cascades, roughly 3,000 machines. Before the June 2025 strikes, Iran’s three declared enrichment facilities contained more than 20,000 centrifuges in 125 full-sized cascades.

The rough estimate needed for one Iranian nuclear weapon is ~100 lbs of U-235 at 60% enrichment or 55 lbs of U-235 at 90% enrichment (modern designs use less.) The difference is important, the lighter the weapon the easier it is to fit on a missile.

At its peak (Feb 2025 to June 2025) Iran’s cascades were delivering ~86 lbs of uranium enriched to 60% which is about 50 lbs of U-235 per month, which is just under one potential weapon every month. (Most weapons use U235 enriched to 90+% because that permits a smaller, more reliable design. Getting to that level in Iran might take days or weeks running the cascades, but building it into a weapon would still be needed.)

Deeply Buried Targets Versus Bunker Busters. One of the stated goals of the U.S. strikes on Iran was to remove their capacity to build nuclear weapons. This required the U.S. to destroy their deeply buried underground nuclear enrichment sites. The largest conventional bomb in the U.S. military’s arsenal is the 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, carried by the B-2 Bomber. A 2019 description said it could reach targets as far as 200 feet underground (its actual effectiveness depends on geology, concrete, facility design, entry points, and the use of multiple weapons). The Iranians knew this and built their nuclear enrichment sites underground. The Fordow site is ~260 to 300 feet under limestone and dolomite. The Natanz site is 25 to 160 feet underground, protected by a 25-foot concrete shield. (But public estimates are over the place.)

Iran declared Isfahan as an enrichment complex to the IAEA the day before the June 2025 strikes; inspectors never got inside it, therefore its depth and geology are unknown, but speculation is that the enrichment complex is 260 to 330 feet underground. Another suspected enrichment facility is in Pickaxe Mountain, where the exact depths, geology, are unknown but estimates put the facility 250 – 330 feet below the summit. Both Isfahan and Pickaxe were Iran’s shift toward "deep mountain basing" to escape the reach of conventional military strikes.

In June 2025 in Operation Midnight Hammer U.S. B-2 bombers dropped 14 GBU-57 bombs on top of Fordow and Natanz. At Isfahan (Esfahan) more than two-dozen submarine-launched Tomahawks hit tunnel entrances and surface targets. In March 2026, strikes at Natanz hit its entrance.

According to the Institute for Science and International Security, the 22,000 centrifuges at Natanz, the Natanz pilot plant, and Fordow are almost certainly wrecked. What may have survived is the enriched uranium, the spare parts, and the people, and that is the problem. The International Atomic Energy Agency estimated (in June 2025) that Iran had about 970 pounds of uranium enriched to 60%; it has since lost track of where it is. Iran's known uranium conversion capability at Isfahan was damaged, which it needed to turn the stockpile of enriched uranium into a weapon, and there is no public evidence that enrichment has resumed at Natanz, Fordow or Isfahan. We never hit Pickaxe Mountain or the Isfahan enrichment facility with the GBU-57. The strikes have set Iran back, but no one knows for how long.

While the GBU-57 MOP cannot cleanly punch through solid rock, the debate has shifted from an absolute physical destruction calculation to a functional denial calculation—meaning the military's goal would be to seal Iran's nuclear assets in a mountain tomb rather than blowing them up directly.

Did We Succeed? Our stated goal was to prevent Iran from rapidly rebuilding the capability to build nuclear weapons, but there’s no certainty that we did that. Repeated airstrikes may have damaged the buried enrichment plants, but we can’t prove it or account for the buried enriched uranium inside. The fact is that it’s extremely difficult to see how much damage the bombs did to Hard and Deeply Buried Targets (HDBTs) from the air, and without inspectors on the ground, knowing for sure is guesswork. Putting boots on the ground would carry enormous costs and risks. Negotiating the removal and inspection of weapons grade uranium would depend on Iranian cooperation and a way to verify we got it all. All bad choices.

There is another emerging option: autonomous drilling equipment.

Subterranean Sensing and Defeat. It’s not hard to imagine that with enough boots on the ground the U.S. could secure a landing zone, fly in drilling equipment and have crews drill hundreds of feet vertically or thousands horizontally to either place sensors and/or explosives. The U.S. has had organizations building specialized equipment and training for breaching tunnels in Combatant Commands and scattered across the DoW for years (DTRA, DARPA, Army ERDC and CAVES and CZ5 programs, SOCOM, Sandia and the Army's half-billion-dollar underground-training push (2018) and ATP 3-21.51 Subterranean Operations.) One can even imagine that there are teams already trained and equipment ready to go. And one can equally imagine the Iranians are waiting for them.

What’s new is autonomous drills that could provide post-strike bomb damage assessments and/or destroy Hard and Deeply Buried Targets (HDBTs) without seizing the site. They might be inserted covertly; more likely they'd need air cover while they work.

The combination of AI, robotics and autonomy moves this from science fiction to the possible.

Anduril, The Boring Company, Exodigo, Phoenix Boring, Earthgrid and Traysar are possible candidates to deliver these systems. There are likely others as well.

(Disclosure: after my first blog about undergrounding critical assets, I invested and have a financial interest in companies in this space.)

Surface survivability and subterranean sensing and defeat are no longer one Service's problem, and they won't be solved by a single system or an incremental fix. Something fundamentally disruptive has changed in the nature of asymmetric warfare and there’s no going back. While we’re actively chasing immediate solutions (Golden Dome, JIATF-401, et al), we need to rethink the nature of force protection, and military and civilian infrastructure protection.

The U.S. needs a coherent protection and survivability strategy across the DoW and all sectors of our economy. This conversation needs to be not only about how we do it, but how we organize it, how we budget and pay for it, and how we rapidly deploy it.
